Static Loads—Static bending moment due to drag for ABL
and uniform flow acquired with the model described in
section 4 is presented in Figure 15 for all wind azimuth
angles. There is a scatter of the static values for a fixed
velocity resulting from the change in azimuth angle for
varying data records. Even with the one small protuberance
mounted at a vehicle azimuth of 180 degrees, there is a
significant change in static coefficients consistent with the
findings of Reference [18]. It should also be noted that
uniform flow data were acquired at additional velocity values
and tunnel conditions in addition to those acquired with an
ABL. Therefore, there is additional scatter in the uniform
flow data that does not have ABL counterpart data.
Plotting these same results for specific wind azimuth angles
and velocities improves clarity and enables a direct
comparison with similar protuberance orientations. Since
there is a single protuberance at 180 degrees, the data should
be symmetrical about the North-South plane and one should
expect higher drag as the protuberance becomes increasingly
orthogonal to the flow.
Static bending moment due to drag acquired at a series of
wind azimuth angle regions are plotted in Figure 16. Each
wind azimuth region considers only those data records
acquired within +/- 15 degrees of the cardinal or ordinal
directions such as N, NE, E, SE and so forth. Data are plotted
adjacent to the corresponding wind azimuth angle when
mirrored about the geometric plane of reflection. As one can
observe, there does appear to be symmetry about 180 degrees.
Furthermore, the static moment is approximately the same
between ABL and uniform flow data. The reasonable
comparison of static magnitude with velocity between ABL
and uniform flow lends confidence to the selection of the
appropriate ABL reference height for velocity comparison.
